newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Opposition strike gets mixed response in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Opposition strike gets mixed response in Pakistan.

text.p: An anti-tax strike called by Pakistani opposition parties and business groups drew a partial response on Saturday, witnesses said.

The main opposition Pakistan Muslim League party had called the strike to protest at last week's 7.86 percent devaluation of the rupee against the dollar and a harsh economic package aimed at securing a resumption of IMF standby loan payments.
An International Monetary Fund mission arrived in Islamabad on Saturday to review the troubled economy with Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's three-year-old government, officials said.
The latest economic measures include additional taxes, among them an agricultural income tax, and a 10 percent increase in fuel prices expected to result in a general rise in prices.
The opposition strike call coincided with one by the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry, unhappy with measures it sees as adding to production costs.
But the protest, billed as a nationwide general strike, was far from total in Pakistan's towns and cities, witnesses said.

Major shopping centres and most private trade and business houses, including foreign currency dealers, stayed shut in the southern port city of Karachi. Public transport was running, but traffic was thinner than usual.
No disturbances were reported in the violence-prone city.

"It is a peaceful day and we have taken normal preventive measures, beefing up security at important places and increased patrolling in volatile parts of the city," Deputy Inspector General of Karachi Police Shoaib Suddle told Reuters.
In the Punjab provincial capital Lahore, big markets were shut, but small foodstores and bakeries stayed open. Some buses, taxis and rickshaws were operating but many stayed off the road.
Some shops were open and some closed in Islamabad, where government offices were shut for the Saturday weekend.

In the nearby city of Rawalpindi, many shops stayed shut, but transport was normal. It was business as usual in the industrial area, where flour mills, a beverage plant and steel mills were all in action, with trucks rolling in and out.
